Newborn Care

Breastfeeding with COVID-19: feeding, precautions and support

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Suspected or confirmed COVID-19 does not usually mean stopping breastfeeding or separating from your baby. If you feel well enough, you can generally keep feeding while reducing respiratory exposure. If illness makes direct feeding difficult, support with expressed milk or another suitable feeding plan can protect both your recovery and your baby's nutrition.

Can COVID-19 pass through breast milk?

Current evidence does not identify breast milk as a source of SARS-CoV-2 transmission to infants. Finding viral genetic material in a sample is not the same as finding live infectious virus or demonstrating infection through milk. The evidence is much broader than the two early case reports discussed in older articles.

A baby can still catch infection through close contact: virus-containing respiratory particles are released when an infected person breathes, talks, coughs or sneezes, even before symptoms or without obvious illness. This risk calls for precautions, not an assumption that the milk is dangerous. Questions about infection during pregnancy or birth are separate from transmission through milk.

Continue feeding when you can

CDC and WHO support breastfeeding with suspected or confirmed COVID-19 when possible, regardless of the mother's vaccination status. COVID-19 alone does not require discarding expressed milk, a routine switch to formula or automatic mother–baby separation. Rooming-in and skin-to-skin contact can usually continue with appropriate precautions and a safe individual care plan.

You deserve practical help and a feeding choice you can manage. A premature or medically vulnerable baby, hospital admission or a very unwell parent may need a specialist plan. If your baby has COVID-19, breastfeeding or expressed milk can usually continue and helps provide fluids; poor feeding or breathing difficulties still need assessment.

Hands, masks and cleaner air

Wash hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds before touching your baby, expressing milk or handling feeding equipment, and after coughing, sneezing or changing a nappy. If unavailable, an alcohol-based hand rub containing at least 60% alcohol is an alternative; let hands dry and keep it out of the baby's reach. Avoid coughing or sneezing onto your baby; use a tissue, dispose of it and clean your hands.

Consider a well-fitting medical mask during close contact, including feeds, when you have or may have COVID-19, following local advice. Change a damp or dirty mask and clean hands when handling it; avoid touching the front. Never put a mask on a baby or any child under two, and keep the baby's face and airway uncovered. Improve indoor ventilation where safe without exposing the baby to unsafe temperatures or hazards. A lack of a mask is not by itself a reason to stop breastfeeding; use the other precautions.

Cleaning without unsafe disinfection

Clean frequently touched household surfaces and follow the cleaning product's label. You do not need to spray everything you touch, cover clothes with alcohol or disinfect feeding items with household surface products. Wash clothing normally. Airborne exposure, hands and correctly cleaned feeding equipment deserve more attention than an old fixed estimate of how many hours virus survives on a surface.

Take apart and clean milk-contact pump parts after each use with suitable dishwashing soap and water, rinse and air-dry thoroughly on a clean surface; clean bottles after feeds. Follow the manufacturer's instructions for boiling, steaming or dishwasher use, and local infant-feeding advice. Sanitize at least daily, especially if your baby is under two months, premature or immunocompromised. For an older healthy baby, daily sanitizing may not be necessary if parts are carefully cleaned after each use. A dishwasher using hot water and a heated drying cycle or sanitizing setting does not require a separate sanitizing step. Never immerse or boil an electric pump's motor; wipe its exterior as directed. Alcohol spray is not a substitute for washing milk residue away.

Expressed milk when direct feeding is difficult

If you are too unwell to feed directly but can express, ask for help to express regularly according to your baby's needs and your comfort. A healthy caregiver can give the milk using an appropriate clean feeding method. Follow safe milk-storage guidance, label containers and avoid contaminating their insides. COVID-19 alone is not a reason to boil, pasteurize or throw away your milk at home.

If expressing is not possible or supply is insufficient, ask about screened donor milk where appropriate and available, or suitable infant formula. Prepare formula with safe water and the exact product proportions, following local guidance and extra precautions for young or vulnerable infants; never dilute it to stretch supplies or use homemade formula. Lactation support can help maintain or rebuild supply. You can resume direct breastfeeding when well enough; there is no universal COVID-related waiting interval, although medicine-specific advice can differ.

Milk antibodies help, but do not guarantee immunity

Breast milk provides nutrition and antibodies and other immune factors. Antibodies to SARS-CoV-2 have been found after infection and vaccination and may help protect infants. This is not guaranteed immunity against infection or severe illness, and does not replace precautions or the child's own recommended vaccinations.

Vaccinations begin according to the child's schedule, not only after breastfeeding ends. COVID-19 vaccination can be given while breastfeeding without routinely interrupting feeds. Ask about current local eligibility, available products and your and your baby's circumstances; recommendations change. Milk antibody findings cannot tell an individual family exactly how much protection their baby has or how long it lasts.

Medicines and the mother's recovery

COVID-19 treatments exist; older statements that none are available are outdated. Seek prompt clinical advice about testing and treatment if you have risk factors or worsening illness: some treatments must start early. Do not withhold needed care solely because you are breastfeeding, or stop essential medicines on your own.

Have a pharmacist or clinician check each medicine, dose, interactions, baby's age and health and possible effects on feeding or supply. Many treatments can be compatible with breastfeeding, but not every medicine is interchangeable or suitable for every infant. Specialist NHS advice on COVID medicines generally concerns healthy term infants; premature or unwell babies need individualized advice. Severe illness requires care and help feeding, not pressure to keep breastfeeding unaided.

Keep closeness and make the plan practical

Prepare clean feeding items, water and tissues within reach; wash your hands and put on the adult mask before settling with your baby when advised. Support the baby's head and keep their nose and mouth unobstructed. Talk gently, make eye contact and respond to feeding cues. Gloves are not routinely needed to open a nursery door or hold your baby and do not replace handwashing.

Ask another adult to handle cleaning, meals or nappy changes if possible. If you become drowsy or exhausted, have someone help: do not fall asleep holding the baby on a sofa or armchair, and return the baby to a separate firm, flat, clear sleep surface on their back. Feeding precautions should support a workable routine and your bond, without blame or unnecessary separation from your infant.

Warning signs in the mother or baby

Seek emergency help immediately for breathing difficulty, persistent chest pain or pressure, new confusion, inability to wake or stay awake, or blue, grey or markedly pale lips or skin in the mother. Seek prompt medical advice if illness worsens, you cannot manage fluids or care safely, or you are concerned; tell services about possible COVID-19 without delaying urgent treatment.

A baby with difficult or paused breathing, blue or grey colour, marked pallor, floppiness, a seizure or difficulty waking needs immediate emergency care. A baby under three months with a temperature of 38°C or higher also needs immediate medical assessment. Get urgent advice for poor feeding or fewer wet nappies; do not wait for a fixed time or a positive COVID test if the baby looks unwell. Not every illness during a household outbreak is COVID-19.

What remains uncertain

Research continues on variants, milk immune responses and the degree and duration of infant protection. Small early studies or a positive milk test cannot answer every transmission question. Current clinical recommendations weigh the benefits of feeding and closeness alongside preventable respiratory exposure and the practical risks of stopping feeds.

Use an individualized plan if circumstances change, particularly with a premature or sick baby, hospital care or a new medication. The usual starting point remains continuing breastfeeding when feasible, adding practical precautions and asking for support. Formula or combined feeding can be part of a safe plan without guilt; COVID-19 itself does not make them automatically safer.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Continue breastfeeding or offer expressed milk if you can, with clean hands and a well-fitting adult mask during close contact when appropriate; never put a mask on your baby.

Ask a clinician or pharmacist to check each medicine, especially if your baby is premature or unwell. Do not automatically stop feeding, discard milk or stop essential treatment.

Clean milk-contact equipment after each use and follow manufacturer instructions for sanitizing and the electrical unit. Get urgent help for warning signs in you or your baby before continuing a feeding routine.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help organize feeding observations and questions. It cannot diagnose COVID-19, assess infant hydration or breathing, guarantee milk immunity or replace prescribing and urgent care.

When to seek help

Never put a mask on an infant. Do not delay emergency care to feed, express, clean equipment or wait for a test. Review medicines individually; do not automatically discard milk or stop essential treatment. Use a safe sleep surface and seek practical feeding help when exhausted or unwell.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • COVID-19 alone usually does not require stopping breastfeeding, discarding milk or separating from your baby.
  • Reduce respiratory exposure with hand hygiene, an adult mask when appropriate and safer ventilation; never mask an infant.
  • Clean milk-contact equipment correctly; do not boil an electric pump motor or spray bottles with surface disinfectant.
  • Milk antibodies may help, but do not guarantee protection or replace vaccination.
  • Review medicines individually and get prompt help for maternal illness or a poorly feeding or unwell baby.

Frequently asked questions

Should I wear a mask while breastfeeding with COVID-19?

Consider a well-fitting medical mask during close contact, following local guidance, alongside clean hands and ventilation. Never put one on the baby. If a mask is unavailable, other precautions and breastfeeding support still matter; lack of a mask alone does not require stopping.

How can I feed if I suspect COVID-19?

You can generally continue direct breastfeeding with precautions if well enough. Alternatively, express regularly if able and have a healthy caregiver offer your milk using clean equipment. Ask for help if neither is manageable.

Can I breastfeed while taking COVID-19 medicine?

Many treatments may be compatible, but the exact drug, dose, interactions and baby's age and health must be checked. Do not assume all drugs require stopping feeds or that all are safe; seek prompt individual prescribing advice.

Can the virus spread through my milk?

Current evidence does not identify milk as a source of transmission. Respiratory close contact can still spread infection. Viral genetic material in a sample is not proof of infectious milk.

Does my milk make my baby immune?

It contains immune factors, including antibodies after infection or vaccination, that may help. They do not guarantee protection; follow precautions and the child's vaccination plan.

Should I discard milk or switch to formula?

Not solely because you have COVID-19. If feeding or expressing is not feasible, discuss donor milk or appropriate formula and safe preparation. Medicine-specific restrictions or a vulnerable infant may change the plan.

What if my baby is ill or not feeding?

Continue breastfeeding or expressed milk if possible, but seek urgent assessment for poor feeding or fewer wet nappies. Breathing problems, abnormal colour, floppiness, difficulty waking or fever of at least 38°C under three months require immediate medical help; do not wait for a test.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
